title: streaming-sse-chunking-backpressure-debug-notes-kyla
content:
Context:
- Investigating intermittent client hangs / truncated streaming responses observed in hosted API (esp. chat streaming via SSE). Reports from PS + internal e2e showed ~0.5-1% of streams either stop emitting mid-response or emit large delayed chunks (bad for low-latency UI).
- Hypothesis: backpressure / chunking interaction between runtime + upstream model process + nginx/proxy + client EventSource, possibly exacerbated by batching / prefix cache.

What I've reproduced locally (env):
- Runtime: local build of serving-runtime (main @ commit 3f4a2d) with streaming SSE handler enabled.
- Model backend: llama-2-13b quantized mimic running in-process (toy) that flushes KV cache in some code paths.
- Proxy: nginx (1.22) configured as reverse proxy to runtime (keepalive on).
- Client: Node.js script (EventSource polyfill) and Chrome EventSource.

Repro commands I ran:
1) Simple curl streaming (raw SSE) to check chunk boundaries:
   curl -v -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" \
     -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/streams 
     -d '{"input":"say a sentence with pauses","stream":true}'
   Observed: sometimes the response stops after a few events; curl still shows connection open but no data for >30s, then a final chunk.

2) Node repro script (attached below) reliably reproduces on my machine ~20% of runs:
   node repro-stream-client.js --concurrency=1 --runs=50

   repro-stream-client.js (short):
   - uses eventsource polyfill
   - listens for "message" and "error" events, logs timestamps and chunk sizes

3) Direct TCP sniff (socat) to inspect raw chunking / Nagle interactions:
   socat - TCP:localhost:8080,raw,rdelay=1
   -> I can see large intervals where no TCP packets are sent from server despite runtime logs indicating tokens generated. Suggests buffering somewhere (maybe nginx or kernel buffer).

Key logs / snippets:
- runtime stdout (trimmed):
  [2026-03-02T15:12:02.123Z] INFO stream-start request_id=abc123 prompt_len=50
  [2026-03-02T15:12:02.145Z] DEBUG tok-gen request_id=abc123 token_idx=1 token="Hello"
  [2026-03-02T15:12:02.146Z] DEBUG tok-gen request_id=abc123 token_idx=2 token=" world"
  [2026-03-02T15:12:02.155Z] DEBUG flush-kv request_id=abc123 reason=cache-miss
  [2026-03-02T15:12:32.200Z] INFO stream-end request_id=abc123 status=ok

  Notice: token generation logged at ~15:12:02 but client doesn't see chunks until ~15:12:32. There's a 30s gap.

- nginx access log (same request):
  10.0.0.5 - - [02/Mar/2026:15:12:02 +0000] "POST /v1/streams HTTP/1.1" 200 512 "-" "curl/7.68.0" 0.000 30.05 0.000
  Fields show upstream_time ~0.000 but request_time 30s. Suggests upstream returned quickly but proxy held response? (or upstream wrote but nginx didn't flush to client).

Hypotheses list (ranked):
1) Nginx buffering: proxy buffering or gzip buffering causing nginx to aggregate small writes until buffer threshold or timeout. Check proxy_buffering off and proxy_http_version 1.1 + chunked_transfer_encoding on.
2) Runtime uses stdio buffering when running model as subprocess (if using std::cout unflushed or FILE* buffering). But our runtime logs show tokens emitted; so logs separate from SSE writes. Need to confirm SSE write path flushes.
3) Kernel/TCP Nagle + small writes + delayed ACKs + proxy interactions causing delay. Some writes may be single small packets that get coalesced; setting TCP_NODELAY on the socket may fix.
4) Client EventSource behavior: Chrome might buffer until a full event delimiter or until a minimum chunk size. But curl -N should show raw behavior; curl shows delay too.
5) Batching/flushing interplay: when KV cache is flushed (see flush-kv log), runtime may perform a blocking operation that delays write until completed; or the runtime writes but then performs a long blocking op and flush isn't actually reaching socket (if using blocking write inside same thread as blocking kernel call).

Quick checks done:
- Turned off nginx (direct to runtime): behaviour still intermittent but frequency reduced -> suggests proxy amplifies but not sole cause.
- Set proxy_buffering off in nginx: reduced incidence but not fully eliminated.
- Enabled TCP_NODELAY on runtime listen socket: reduced incidence further.
- Changed runtime to call socket.write(..., "utf8") + socket.uncork()/flush (node-like) in C++ we added explicit flush after write. This reduced rate but did not eliminate.
- Reproduced with python SSE server (aiohttp) + same nginx config -> no issue (in ~100 runs). This points to implementation detail in our runtime (threading / blocking inside token generation).

Additional observations:
- When reproduction occurs, runtime logs show tokens being generated in separate worker threads, but SSE handler's write calls happen on the main accept thread (or an actor) and may be serialized via a write queue. If a worker triggers a synchronous op (e.g., fsync to disk, heavy malloc) right after writing, flush to socket might be blocked.
- Memory allocator patterns: spikes in malloc/free correlate with some bad runs. Might be locking/blocking in jemalloc.

Next actions / TODOs:
1) Instrument the runtime SSE path to record precise timestamps for: token ready -> write call -> kernel send() syscalls -> write completion. Add tracepoints around send()/write() to measure time spent in syscall and whether data leaves kernel buffer.
2) Run packet capture (tcpdump) aligned to request to see exact packets emitted vs token gen times. Correlate with process-level strace to show send calls.
3) Try alternate allocator (malloc mimalloc) build to see if reduced locking helps.
4) Create minimal repro that doesn't use model: runtime returns generated tokens from an in-memory generator at same pacing; if problem persists, it's likely networking/proxy.
5) Add explicit flush/flush-after-each-event in SSE code path and test with high QPS.
6) Add per-connection backlog metrics and socket buffer occupancy metrics (SO_SNDBUF usage) in runtime to detect when socket buffers are filling.

Immediate mitigations for customers:
- Recommend setting proxy_buffering off and ensure keepalive timeouts are > 60s.
- Set TCP_NODELAY on custom proxies or suggest bypassing nginx for latency-critical streams.

Notes for ticket INF-345 (linked):
- Include packet captures and strace output from my repro runs (saved in /tmp/kyla-stream-debug).
- Summarize: proxy + runtime write path interplay + blocking operations are most likely root cause.

Unresolved questions:
- Why does nginx upstream_time show ~0.000 when runtime logs show tokens generated early? Is nginx only reporting time to first byte or to upstream request completion? Need to check nginx log format used here.
- Is there any interaction with our internal streaming middleware (rate-limiter) that batches writes? I haven't found code path but will audit middleware chain.

Appendix: quick repro notes for engineers
- Node client: repro-stream-client.js (uses eventsource)
- Run with no proxy:
  ./bazel run //cmd/serving-runtime -- --port=8080 &
  node repro-stream-client.js --runs=200
- Run via nginx (example conf snippet):
  location /v1/streams {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
    proxy_set_header Connection ""; # allow keepalive
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_buffering off;
    chunked_transfer_encoding on;
  }

- Packet capture (for one request):
  sudo tcpdump -i lo -w /tmp/stream.pcap port 8080 and host 127.0.0.1

If anyone picks this up: start with instrumentation to get syscall-level timing (send/write) + tcpdump + confirm whether nginx still aggregates despite proxy_buffering off. Samir/Ava, ping me if you want the strace/tcptrace outputs I already collected.

Notes-to-self: possible quick-fix is to have runtime coalesce small tokens into slightly larger writes (e.g., aggregate up to 1KB or 10ms window) to avoid Nagle/delayed-ACK edge cases. But must balance latency.

End.
